newsitem.title: USA: Taxable bonds in mix for proposed Illinois airport.
newsitem.headline: Taxable bonds in mix for proposed Illinois airport.

text.p: A public-private development of a new airport southwest of Chicago would involve the initial issuance of taxable general airport revenue bonds, a state official said Friday.
Kirk Brown, Illinois secretary of transportation, said that under financing options that include private participation, the bonds would initially sold on a taxable basis.

After the facility was built, the debt would be refinanced with tax-exempt and taxable debt, Brown said, pointing out that portions such as the airfield would qualify for tax-free financing, while debt for a parking garage would be taxable.

The private financing options unveiled by the state Friday would carry price tags totaling $288 million to $361 million with the private share of the cost pegged at only $17 million to $13 million. The rest of the funding would come largely from the issuance of $258 million to $356 million of GARBs, as well as $67 million to $104 million of federal aviation funds.

Brown said that under the puplic-private scenario, which he said would be the first for a U.S. airport, the state may have to contribute money for land acquisition. That plan envisions that all financing, construction and operation of the airport would be handled by a private partner.
Brown said that state officials would meet with private entities to discuss things such as risk sharing, equitable funding and control issues.
State transportation officials also outlined public financing options for the airport Gov. Jim Edgar proposed in 1991 to build in Peotone, a town about 35 miles southwest of Chicago.

A hub airport under that scenario would cost $2.7 billion, financed with $2.5 billion of bonds and $225 million of federal funds. A non-hub airport would cost $416 million with $320 million of bonds and $96 million of federal funds.
Brown said that a local or regional airport authority would probably have to be created by the General Assembly to finance and run the airport.
Any of the financing options faces an uphill struggle.
A draft environmental impact statement for the airport has languished at the Federal Aviation Administration, which still has the plan under review, according to a spokesman.
In addition, Brown said not a single airline has expressed interest in the plan, which would rely mainly on agreements with the carriers to pay off the largest financing component -- the bonds.
In fact, airlines and their trade group, the Air Transport Association, have been vocal in their opposition to the airport.

The state also lacks a regional consensus that another airport is needed, as Chicago Mayor Richard Daley, who controls O'Hare International and Midway airports, has publicly attacked both the need and the feasibility of financing the facility.
Still, Brown contended that the Chicago region was running out of air capacity and would eventually face the loss of its standing as an air transportation center.
"If we don't do something about air capacity, we're going to be a third-rate city," Brown said.
